subject: ela
skillName: Write routinely for a range of tasks and audiences
intro: Strong writers write often, and they adjust how they write to fit the task, the purpose, and the audience. A quick journal entry, a short answer for science class, and a letter to a city official all sound different even when written by the same person. This lesson shows how to shift your length, tone, and detail to match what each writing situation needs.

items.prompt: Write a short journal entry (3 to 4 sentences) describing a moment from your day. Purpose: reflection for yourself. Audience: just you. Use the prompt: 'A small thing that changed my mood today.'

steps: A journal entry for yourself can be informal and personal.
Focus on one small moment and how it made you feel.
Include a specific detail so the memory stays clear.
solution.answer: This morning I was dreading the math quiz, and my stomach felt tight all through breakfast. Then I found a sticky note from my sister stuck to my binder that said 'You've got this.' It was such a tiny thing, but I smiled the whole walk to school. I did not even mind the quiz that much after that.

items.prompt: Write a short explanatory paragraph (4 to 5 sentences) for a science class. Purpose: explain a process clearly. Audience: classmates. Topic: why ice floats on water.

steps: For a science explanation, use a clear topic sentence and accurate details.
Keep the tone informative, not casual.
End with a sentence that sums up the main idea.
solution.answer: Ice floats on water because it is less dense than the liquid water around it. When water freezes, its molecules arrange themselves into an open, hexagonal pattern with extra space between them. This means a block of ice takes up more room than the same amount of liquid water, so it weighs less for its size. Because the ice is lighter than the water it would replace, it rises to the surface and floats. This unusual property is why ponds freeze from the top down instead of the bottom up.

items.prompt: Write a brief, polite email (3 to 5 sentences) to a teacher. Purpose: request something. Audience: an adult in authority. Situation: you need to ask Ms. Carter if you can make up a lab you missed while sick.

steps: An email to a teacher should be polite and use formal language.
State your purpose clearly and give the needed details.
Close with a thank you.
solution.answer: Dear Ms. Carter, I am writing because I was absent on Tuesday with the flu and missed the density lab. I would like to ask whether I could make it up after school this week or during a study period. Please let me know what time would work best for you. Thank you for your help.

items.prompt: Write a short compare-and-contrast paragraph (4 to 6 sentences). Purpose: show similarities and differences. Audience: classmates. Topic: reading a book versus watching its movie version.

steps: Decide on two or three points to compare.
Use signal words like 'both,' 'however,' and 'while' to show comparison.
Make sure each subject gets balanced attention.
solution.answer: Reading a book and watching its movie both tell the same basic story, but the experience is very different. A book lets you hear a character's private thoughts and imagine the setting in your own way, which can make the story feel personal. A movie, however, shows everything at once with actors, music, and scenery, so it moves faster and feels more dramatic. While a book might take a week to finish, a movie is over in about two hours. Both can be enjoyable, but each one asks the audience to use their imagination in a different way.

items.prompt: Write a short persuasive note (4 to 5 sentences). Purpose: convince. Audience: your school principal. Situation: argue for adding a few minutes to lunch.

steps: Persuasive writing for an authority figure should be respectful and reasoned.
State a clear claim and give at least one solid reason.
End with a courteous request.
solution.answer: Dear Principal Nguyen, I would like to suggest adding five minutes to our lunch period. Right now many students must rush through eating to make it to their next class, and some end up throwing away food they did not have time to finish. A slightly longer lunch would help students eat properly and return to class focused instead of hungry. I hope you will consider this small change, and thank you for listening to student ideas.

items.prompt: Write a quick journal entry (3 to 4 sentences). Purpose: reflection. Audience: yourself. Prompt: 'Something I tried for the first time recently.'
items.hint: Keep it personal and informal. Name the specific thing you tried and how it felt.

steps: Pick one specific new experience.
Describe what happened and your honest reaction.
It is fine to use a casual, personal tone.
solution.answer: Last weekend I tried rock climbing at the new gym, and I was honestly terrified of falling. My hands were shaking on the first wall, but my friend kept cheering from below until I reached the top. When I looked down, I could not believe how high I had climbed. I think I want to go back next week and try a harder route.

items.prompt: Write a short explanatory paragraph (4 to 5 sentences) for a history class. Purpose: explain clearly. Audience: classmates. Topic: why ancient people settled near rivers.
items.hint: Use a clear topic sentence and give two or three concrete reasons.

steps: Begin with a topic sentence stating the main idea.
Give specific reasons with accurate detail.
Use an informative tone.
solution.answer: Ancient people often settled near rivers because rivers provided the resources needed to survive. The water could be used for drinking, cooking, and watering crops, which made farming possible. Rivers also offered fish to eat and a route for traveling and trading with other communities. In addition, the soil along riverbanks was rich and fertile, so crops grew well there. For all these reasons, many of the world's first cities grew up along great rivers.

items.prompt: Write a brief, polite email (3 to 5 sentences) to a librarian. Purpose: request help. Audience: an adult. Situation: ask Mr. Davis to help you find sources for a research project on renewable energy.
items.hint: Be polite and formal. State clearly what you need help with.

steps: Open with a respectful greeting.
Explain your purpose and give useful details.
Close with thanks.
solution.answer: Dear Mr. Davis, I am working on a research project about renewable energy and I am having trouble finding reliable sources. Could you help me find a few books or trusted websites about solar and wind power? I am free to come to the library during lunch or after school this week. Thank you very much for your help.

items.prompt: Write a short compare-and-contrast paragraph (4 to 6 sentences). Purpose: show similarities and differences. Audience: classmates. Topic: summer versus winter.
items.hint: Choose two or three points to compare, and use signal words like 'both,' 'while,' and 'however.'

steps: Pick clear points of comparison such as weather and activities.
Give balanced attention to both seasons.
Use comparison signal words.
solution.answer: Summer and winter are opposite seasons, but both have their own appeal. Summer brings long, warm days that are perfect for swimming, biking, and spending time outdoors. Winter, however, is cold and dark earlier, which makes it a good time for indoor activities like reading or building a fire. While summer invites people outside, winter often draws families together indoors. Both seasons offer holidays and a break from school, so each one has something to look forward to.

items.prompt: Write a short persuasive paragraph (4 to 6 sentences). Purpose: convince. Audience: your classmates. Situation: argue that your class should choose a community garden as its service project.
items.hint: State a clear claim, give at least two reasons, and speak directly to your classmates.

steps: State your claim in the first sentence.
Support it with reasons your audience would care about.
End with a call to action.
solution.answer: Our class should choose a community garden as our service project this year. A garden would give us a hands-on way to work together outside instead of sitting at desks. It would also provide fresh vegetables for families in our neighborhood who need them, so our work would help real people. Best of all, a garden keeps growing long after we plant it, which means our project would leave a lasting mark on the community. Let's vote for the garden and create something we can all be proud of.
